interest: Japan's Kunrei-shiki romanization rollout, its headaches for consular records, and Japanese displacing English in North China schools as cultural imperialism.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.402, File 1202) covers records from November 1931 through August 1940 pertaining to social matters involving the Japanese language, particularly romanization reforms, language pedagogy, and consular administration. A substantial portion of the correspondence and reporting centers on the Japanese Government's September 1937 Cabinet Order No. 3, which officially decreed the adoption of the Kunrei-shiki/Kokuritsu romanization system ("Romazi") over the long-established Hepburn system, analyzing the resultant domestic debates, phonetic rationale, and complications for U.S. visa, passport, and immigrant identification records. Alongside these orthographic developments, the collection includes inquiries and detailed embassy recommendations concerning Japanese kanji textbooks and dictionaries for American students, diplomatic tensions and miscommunications stemming from linguistic nuances, and the geopolitical projection of the Japanese language into occupied North China (such as Peiping) where Japanese was mandated in schools and rapidly displaced English in commerce.
